walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme 2: The UK Economy - Performance and Policies — a core area of A-Level Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme 2: The UK Economy - Performance and Policies brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme 2: The UK Economy - Performance and Policies.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The Laffer curve was popularised in:
Solow's growth model shows long-run growth driven by:
options: Capital accumulation
Technological progress
Population growth
Government spending

mcqs.q: What defines a pure public good?
options: Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
A public good is anything provided by the government.
A public good is anything that's free.
Non-rivalry (one person's use doesn't reduce others') and non-excludability (you can't stop people benefiting) — e.g. national defence, street lighting.

mcqs.q: What components make up aggregate demand?
options: Aggregate demand is just the total amount consumers want to buy.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
AD = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. A shift in any component shifts the AD curve.

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.
A public good is anything that's free.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
